title: The Garden next door
hookLine: Epicurus taught in a garden: simple pleasures, friends, and freedom from fear (Diogenes Laërtius 10)

lines: A POT OF CHEESE WAS A FEAST.
cards: Say the word epicurean today and people picture a tasting menu: truffles, a wine list, a chef with tweezers. The man the word comes from would have been baffled.

He lived very plainly and thought a little pot of cheese was a feast. And while the Stoics argued in a busy public porch in the middle of Athens, he and his friends were outside the city walls, in a garden.
Two schools, same city, around the same time, very different answers.

teach.b: First, the place. Epicurus settled in Athens and bought a garden, just outside the city. His school became known simply as the Garden, the way Zeno's became the Porch.
It was more like a community than a lecture hall. Friends lived and ate together, and Diogenes Laërtius names women and at least one enslaved man among the circle. Second, the goal.
Epicurus taught that the aim of life is pleasure. That's the word that scandalized people then and misleads people now. He meant something quiet: no pain in the body, and no turmoil in the mind.
The Greek for that inner calm is ataraxia, being untroubled. He thought much of our misery comes from wanting things we don't need and fearing things we needn't fear. Third, the fears.

teach.h: NO FEAR OF GODS OR DEATH.
teach.b: The two big ones, he said, are fear of the gods and fear of death.
Epicureans held that the gods exist but don't punish or meddle, and that the world is made of atoms moving in the void, so death is simply the end of feeling.

The Stoics disagreed sharply, believing in a providential reason running through all things. Both schools sought a calm mind; they drew different maps to it, and each had thoughtful followers for centuries.

teach.h: FRIENDS ARE MOST OF THE MEAL.
teach.b: Fourth, the heart of the Garden: friends. Simple food, shared.
Conversation. People who know you. For Epicurus, that was not a side dish to the good life.
It was most of the meal.

how: Epicureans, ancient and modern, practice a simple life centered on friendship, modest pleasures and freedom from fear, often gathering to share plain meals and conversation.

o: a total absence of all feeling
an untroubled calm, free of fear
a life of rich food and fine wine

games.q: the Garden next door. tap the pairs.

s: Epicurus taught that the good life means luxury and fine dining
he meant no pain in body, no turmoil in mind; he lived very plainly.
the Garden included women among its members
Diogenes Laërtius names women in Epicurus's circle.
Epicureans believed the gods punish wrongdoers after death
they held the gods don't meddle and death is the end of feeling.

games.q: you're Epicurus, newly in Athens, ready to teach. where do you set up?
o: a busy public porch in the marketplace.
a garden outside the city, with friends living together.
games.why: Epicurus bought a garden outside the walls, and his school became a community of friends: the Garden.

practice: Think of one simple pleasure you could share with a friend: a coffee on a bench, a walk around the block, a bowl of soup, a phone call while you both fold laundry.
Picture the friend and the place, and notice whether the pleasure needs anything you don't already have. Usually it doesn't.

wordCard.voice: Ataraxia. Epicurus's word for the untroubled calm his Garden sought, free of fear of the gods and of death. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: garden. The name of Epicurus's school, as the Stoa (porch) named Zeno's.

carryVoice: Your line: the garden. Pleasure, for Epicurus, meant quiet, not luxury. Six hundred fifty days now.

sources.work: Diogenes Laërtius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers
